title: Connection Pooling Strategies
description: Pool and manage Redis connections efficiently across threads, workers, and serverless functions.

data.text: Each Redis client instance opens a single TCP socket. In a high-throughput service, that one connection becomes a bottleneck: Redis processes commands sequentially, so concurrent requests queue behind it. Connection pooling gives your application multiple sockets, enabling true parallel command execution and dramatically improving throughput.

Redis processes commands on a single thread per instance, but it achieves concurrency by multiplexing across many client connections. Each active connection contributes one command at a time. A single client can therefore issue multiple pipelined commands, but only one is in flight per socket. More connections mean more concurrent work.

data.caption: Multiple Node.js clients sharing a pool of Redis sockets

data.text: ioredis does not include a built-in connection pool, but you can create one using `generic-pool`, a minimal Node.js pool implementation. Each pool entry holds a pre-connected Redis client. When your code needs Redis, it borrows a client, uses it, then returns it to the pool.

data.title: Building a Redis connection pool
data.content: Use generic-pool to manage Redis client instances.

data.text: Pool size directly affects Redis memory and CPU usage. Each connection consumes about 40 KB of memory on the Redis server. The practical formula is: max connections equals the number of Node.js application instances multiplied by the number of concurrent request handlers per instance, capped at your Redis instance's `maxclients` limit (default 10,000 on most managed providers).

rows: Warm containers share pools across invocations

data.title: Avoid Over-Provisioning
data.text: Setting max connections to 100 when your workload only needs 10 wastes Redis memory and increases the chance of hitting maxclients during failover. Start small and measure.

In serverless environments, connection reuse across warm invocations is the key to low latency. A pool initialized at module scope persists for the lifetime of the warm container. Set min to 1-2 so the pool stays warm between invocations, and max to 3-5 to avoid opening too many connections during sudden traffic spikes.

data.title: Serverless-ready pool initialization
data.content: Initialize the pool once at module scope for Lambda reuse.

terms.definition: A collection of pre-initialized connections that can be borrowed and returned, avoiding the overhead of creating a new socket per operation.

items.question: Should I use connection pooling for every Redis client?
items.answer: Use pooling when your application handles concurrent requests or runs multiple instances. For simple scripts or CLI tools, a single client is fine.

items.question: What happens if the pool is exhausted?
items.answer: generic-pool returns a promise that resolves when another client is released. Use a timeout to avoid hanging indefinitely.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Each Redis client uses one TCP socket; pooling enables parallel commands.
Size pools based on actual concurrent request volume, not maximum possible load.
In serverless, initialize the pool once at module scope for warm-container reuse.
Monitor Redis maxclients and scale your pool before reaching the limit.
